title: A clean place, a firm seat
hook: on a battlefield, Krishna gives meditation instructions exact enough to follow tonight: the place, the seat, the mind on God
carry: a clean place, a firm seat, the mind on God
tomorrow: The lamp in a windless place

segments.voice: Yesterday, lift the self by the self. Today, where and how to sit.

A strange setting for a meditation class: two armies, conch shells blown, and a warrior who has just said he can't fight. And right there, Krishna gives Arjuna instructions so exact you could follow them tonight. Not vague ones. Where to sit. What to sit on. How high. How to hold your head. Where to put your eyes. And then a line that surprises people: how much to eat and sleep.
screen: `TWO ARMIES. CONCH SHELLS.` → `A MEDITATION CLASS.` → `WHERE, WHAT, HOW HIGH.`

segments.voice: Verse ten starts with the place. The yogi should sit alone, somewhere apart, with body and mind under control, not grasping. Verse eleven: in a clean place, set a firm seat, not too high and not too low. In the old instructions it's layered: sacred kusha grass, a deerskin, cloth. For most people now, a folded blanket or a steady chair. Verse twelve: sitting there, make the mind one-pointed and practice yoga to purify yourself. Verse thirteen, the posture: body, head and neck in a straight line, still and steady, the gaze toward the tip of the nose, not looking around. And verse fourteen, the heart of it: calm, without fear, the mind held, sitting with the mind on Krishna, intent on him. That's the Hindu teaching here. Meditation, dhyana, isn't only a calm-down trick. It's yoga, joining the mind to God, and the place is part of it. It's why so many Hindu homes keep a clean corner or a small shrine set apart, and why people take off their shoes before they sit there. Then the balance. Yoga, verse sixteen says, isn't for someone who eats too much or not at all, who sleeps too much or stays awake too long. Moderate in food and rest, in effort, in sleep: then yoga destroys sorrow. Today, look at your room. A bed, a desk, a charger. Is there one spot kept only for this?
screen: `A CLEAN PLACE, A FIRM SEAT.` · `BODY, HEAD, NECK IN A LINE.` · `THE MIND ON GOD.` · `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT TOO LITTLE.` · then, large: `A PLACE SET APART.`

segments.voice: Find the steadiest seat near you, a chair or a folded blanket on the floor, not too high and not too low, and let body, head and neck line up, as if a thread lifts the top of your head. Lower and soften the eyes toward the tip of the nose, stop looking around, and stay still. You can hold Krishna in mind, as verse fourteen says, or, if that isn't your way, hold the stillness itself.
Asana. The seat, and the way of sitting. The Gita's instructions: a clean place, a firm seat, body and head and neck in a line, the mind on God, and moderation in food and sleep.
Carry this: a clean place, a firm seat, the mind on God. Not too high, not too low, not too much. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a clean corner or home shrine for daily sitting, often on a mat or cloth, with a straight spine and a steady gaze, following the pattern of Gita 6.10–6.17.

notes: 6.11's layering order (kusha, deerskin, cloth) is stated from the usual reading of 'cailajina-kushottaram'; commentators differ on which is on top. The voice avoids stating which is on top.
6.14 also mentions the vow of brahmacharya (celibacy); left out for a general audience. Keeper may want it named.
'Gaze toward the tip of the nose' (nasikagram): some commentators read it as a half-closed, inward gaze rather than literal looking. Confirm.
